summary.text: Set \(M=(2n+1)^2=2t+1\) with \(t=2n(n+1)\), and iterate \(F(x)=(x-t)^2\mathbin{\mathrm{AND}}M\) from \(0\); because \(4\mid t\), all iterates are divisible by \(16\), and congruence modulo \(2^r\) is improved by \(F\) to congruence modulo \(2^{r+3}\), so boundedness by \(M\) eventually forces a fixed point. Using \(a\operatorname{XOR}b+2(a\mathbin{\mathrm{AND}}b)=a+b\) and \(M=2t+1\), that fixed point yields a witness by taking \(k=t-x\) if \(x\le t\), and \(k=x-t-1\) otherwise.

full_proof.text:
We prove that for every natural number \(n\) there is a natural number \(k\) such that
\[
 k^2\operatorname{XOR}(k+1)^2=(2n+1)^2.
\]
Consequently, the set from which \(a(n)\) is chosen is nonempty; by well-ordering it has a least member, so the OEIS value is never \(-1\).

Throughout, write \(u\mathbin{\&}v\) for the bitwise AND of two nonnegative integers and \(u\oplus v\) for their bitwise XOR.

We begin with two elementary facts about binary operations.

First,
\[
 (a\oplus b)+2(a\mathbin{\&}b)=a+b                       \tag{1}
\]
for all nonnegative integers \(a,b\). Indeed, at each binary position, if the corresponding bits of \(a,b\) are \(\alpha,\beta\in\{0,1\}\), then
\[
 (\alpha\mathbin{\mathrm{XOR}}\beta)+2\alpha\beta=\alpha+\beta.
\]
Multiplying this equality by the appropriate power of two and summing over all bit positions gives (1).

Second, bitwise AND respects congruences modulo powers of two: if
\[
 a\equiv b\pmod {2^r},
\]
then, for every \(M\),
\[
 a\mathbin{\&}M\equiv b\mathbin{\&}M\pmod {2^r}.          \tag{2}
\]
This is because congruence modulo \(2^r\) says exactly that the lowest \(r\) binary digits of \(a\) and \(b\) agree, and AND with \(M\) acts on each digit separately. We will also use the immediate bound
\[
 a\mathbin{\&}M\le M,                                     \tag{3}
\]
since every nonzero bit of \(a\mathbin{\&}M\) is also a nonzero bit of \(M\).

Now fix \(n\ge 0\), and define
\[
 M=(2n+1)^2,
 \qquad
 t=2n(n+1).
\]
Expanding the square gives the important relation
\[
 M=4n^2+4n+1=2t+1.                                        \tag{4}
\]
Also,
\[
 4\mid t.                                                  \tag{5}
\]
Indeed, one of \(n,n+1\) is even, so \(n(n+1)\) is even, and hence \(2n(n+1)\) is divisible by \(4\).

For a nonnegative integer \(x\), define its squared distance from \(t\) by
\[
 D(x)=|x-t|^2
 =\begin{cases}
 (t-x)^2,&x\le t,\\
 (x-t)^2,&x>t.
 \end{cases}
\]
Define the masked squared-distance map
\[
 F(x)=D(x)\mathbin{\&}M.                                  \tag{6}
\]
Starting with \(x_0=0\), iterate this map:
\[
 x_{j+1}=F(x_j)\qquad(j\ge0).                              \tag{7}
\]
We will prove that this iteration reaches a fixed point.

First, every iterate is divisible by \(16\):
\[
 16\mid x_j\qquad\text{for every }j\ge0.                  \tag{8}
\]
This follows by induction. It is true for \(x_0=0\). Suppose \(16\mid x_j\). In particular, \(4\mid x_j\), while (5) gives \(4\mid t\). Therefore \(x_j-t\), or equivalently its absolute value, is divisible by \(4\), so its square \(D(x_j)\) is divisible by \(16\). Thus the lowest four bits of \(D(x_j)\) are zero. Taking a bitwise AND with \(M\) cannot turn any of those bits into a one, so \(16\mid F(x_j)=x_{j+1}\). This proves (8).

Next we establish a contraction property in the binary, or \(2\)-adic, sense. Suppose that \(x,y\) are both divisible by \(16\), that \(4\mid t\), and that
\[
 x\equiv y\pmod {2^r}.
\]
Viewing the squared distances as ordinary integer squares, we have
\[
 D(x)=(x-t)^2,
 \qquad
 D(y)=(y-t)^2;

the signs hidden by the absolute values do not matter after squaring. Their difference factors as
\[
 D(y)-D(x)
 =(y-t)^2-(x-t)^2
 =(y-x)(x+y-2t).                                           \tag{9}
\]
The first factor is divisible by \(2^r\). The second factor is divisible by \(8\): both \(x\) and \(y\) are divisible by \(16\), and \(2t\) is divisible by \(8\) because \(4\mid t\). Hence (9) is divisible by \(2^{r+3}\), so
\[
 D(x)\equiv D(y)\pmod {2^{r+3}}.
\]
Applying (2), with modulus \(2^{r+3}\), yields
\[
 F(x)\equiv F(y)\pmod {2^{r+3}}.                          \tag{10}
\]
Thus applying \(F\) to two multiples of \(16\) increases their number of guaranteed matching low binary digits by three.

We apply (10) to consecutive iterates. We claim that for every \(j\ge0\),
\[
 x_{j+1}\equiv x_j\pmod {2^{4+3j}}.                       \tag{11}
\]
For \(j=0\), both \(x_1\) and \(x_0\) are divisible by \(16=2^4\), by (8), so the claim holds. If it holds for \(j\), then \(x_{j+1}\) and \(x_j\) are both divisible by \(16\), again by (8). Applying (10) with \(r=4+3j\) gives
\[
 F(x_{j+1})\equiv F(x_j)\pmod {2^{4+3j+3}}.
\]
By the recurrence (7), this is
\[
 x_{j+2}\equiv x_{j+1}\pmod {2^{4+3(j+1)}},
\]
which proves the induction step and hence (11).

All positive-index iterates are bounded by \(M\). Indeed, from (3) and (6),
\[
 x_{j+1}=D(x_j)\mathbin{\&}M\le M                         \tag{12}
\]
for every \(j\ge0\).

Take \(j=M+1\) in (11). We obtain
\[
 x_{M+2}\equiv x_{M+1}\pmod {2^{4+3(M+1)}}.               \tag{13}
\]
The modulus in (13) is larger than \(M\). For example,
\(4+3(M+1)\ge M+1\), and the elementary inequality
\(2^{M+1}>M\) gives
\[
 2^{4+3(M+1)}>M.
\]
By (12), both \(x_{M+2}\) and \(x_{M+1}\) lie between \(0\) and \(M\). Two numbers in this interval that are congruent modulo an integer larger than \(M\) must be equal. Therefore
\[
 x_{M+2}=x_{M+1}.                                         \tag{14}
\]
Set
\[
 x=x_{M+1}.
\]
Using (7), equality (14) says precisely that
\[
 x=F(x)=D(x)\mathbin{\&}M.                                \tag{15}
\]
Also \(x\le M\) by (12), although only the fixed-point identity will be needed in the algebra below.

It remains to turn this fixed point into the required \(k\). There are two cases, according to which side of \(t\) the fixed point lies.

**Case 1: \(x\le t\).**

Put
\[
 k=t-x.
\]
Then \(k\ge0\), and since \(D(x)=(t-x)^2=k^2\), equation (15) becomes
\[
 k^2\mathbin{\&}M=x.                                      \tag{16}
\]
Apply identity (1) to \(k^2\) and \(M\). Using (16),
\[
 (k^2\oplus M)+2x=k^2+M.                                  \tag{17}
\]
On the other hand, because \(k+x=t\) and \(M=2t+1\),
\[
 (k+1)^2+2x
 =k^2+2k+1+2x
 =k^2+2(k+x)+1
 =k^2+2t+1
 =k^2+M.                                                   \tag{18}
\]
Comparing (17) and (18), and cancelling \(2x\), gives
\[
 k^2\oplus M=(k+1)^2.                                     \tag{19}
\]
XOR is associative and commutative, and every number is its own inverse under XOR: \(u\oplus u=0\). XORing (19) with \(k^2\) therefore yields
\[
 M=k^2\oplus(k+1)^2,
\]
as desired.

**Case 2: \(x>t\).**

Now put
\[
 k=x-t-1.
\]
The strict inequality \(x>t\) ensures that \(k\ge0\), and
\[
 k+1=x-t.
\]
Since in this case \(D(x)=(x-t)^2=(k+1)^2\), the fixed-point equation (15) gives
\[
 (k+1)^2\mathbin{\&}M=x.                                  \tag{20}
\]
Applying (1) to \((k+1)^2\) and \(M\), and using (20), gives
\[
 ((k+1)^2\oplus M)+2x=(k+1)^2+M.                          \tag{21}
\]
Here \(x=t+k+1\). Together with \(M=2t+1\), this implies
\[
 (k+1)^2+M
 =k^2+2k+1+2t+1
 =k^2+2(t+k+1)
 =k^2+2x.                                                  \tag{22}
\]
Comparing (21) and (22), and cancelling \(2x\), yields
\[
 (k+1)^2\oplus M=k^2.                                     \tag{23}
\]
XORing appropriately and using associativity, commutativity, and \(u\oplus u=0\), equation (23) is equivalent to
\[
 k^2\oplus(k+1)^2=M.
\]
Thus this case also produces the required nonnegative integer \(k\).

In both cases we have found \(k\in\mathbb N\) satisfying
\[
 k^2\operatorname{XOR}(k+1)^2=M=(2n+1)^2.
\]
Since \(n\) was arbitrary, such a \(k\) exists for every \(n\ge0\). Hence the defining candidate set for A224515 is always nonempty, proving the existence conjecture.
